comparison: Both address the main conclusion (C10-C12, C169) that boundary-pairing drives TAD formation. OpenEval finds this SUPPORTED by multiple lines of evidence, while peer reviewers rate it UNCERTAIN, noting that loop extruders were not experimentally depleted and that the two models are not mutually exclusive.

Both discuss the absence of loop-extrusion signatures (stripes) in MicroC data (C86, C99, C103, C149-C151). OpenEval considers this SUPPORTED critical negative evidence against loop extrusion, while Reviewer 4 rates it UNCERTAIN, questioning whether stripes would actually appear even if loop extrusion occurred, requesting validation from organisms known to undergo loop extrusion.

Both address the eve TAD structure from MicroC data (C80-C83). OpenEval finds the stem-loop topology SUPPORTED, and peer reviewers also accept this structural characterization as SUPPORTED, with the editor noting the evidence for boundary pairing is compelling.

Both discuss orientation-dependent transgene expression patterns (C124-C126, C130-C141). OpenEval finds these SUPPORTED as critical tests distinguishing models, and peer reviewers also rate them SUPPORTED, with Reviewer 3 calling the transgenic experiments 'extensive and elegant.'

Both address correlation between MicroC interactions and functional activation (C145-C148, C152-C159). OpenEval finds this SUPPORTED, and peer reviewers agree (SUPPORTED), with Reviewer 2 confirming that '3D DNA contacts confirm that transgene expression correlates with the contacts.'

Both discuss the synthesis of findings across all transgene orientations (C165-C168). OpenEval finds this SUPPORTED, and peer reviewers also rate it SUPPORTED, noting the comprehensive coverage of all orientation combinations.

Both address the GhomieL transgene results showing dual activation (C134-C135). OpenEval finds this SUPPORTED as definitively ruling out loop extrusion, while peer reviewers rate it UNCERTAIN, noting that imaging data 'seems to support both loop extrusion and the boundary:boundary models.'

Both discuss the homie fragment composition and function (C108-C109). OpenEval finds the established findings SUPPORTED, while Reviewer 4 rates it UNCERTAIN, questioning why homie orientation matters when the CTCF motif is not present in the transgene.

Both address live imaging data showing correlation between proximity and activation (C114-C117). OpenEval finds this SUPPORTED, while Reviewer 4 rates it UNCERTAIN, noting that the exact transgenes used in this study may not have been measured for distance in the cited Chen et al. 2018 study.

Both discuss mechanisms for LDC domain formation in the boundary-pairing model (C104-C105, C92, C94, C97, C186-C187). OpenEval rates the proposed mechanisms UNCERTAIN as speculative, while peer reviewers rate the observations SUPPORTED, not challenging the mechanistic proposals.

Both address the generalizability of boundary pairing beyond homie/nhomie (C170-C175). OpenEval finds this SUPPORTED by extensive literature, and peer reviewers also rate it SUPPORTED, with Reviewer 3 acknowledging the authors repeat previous work establishing boundary pairing properties.

Both discuss genomic examples of boundary pairing at Lar and beat IV loci (C176-C182). OpenEval finds this SUPPORTED as independent validation, and peer reviewers also rate it SUPPORTED, not challenging these meta-loop observations.

Both address the interpretation that circle-loops predominate in the eve neighborhood (C183, C185). OpenEval rates this UNCERTAIN as somewhat speculative, while peer reviewers rate it SUPPORTED, though Reviewer 3 notes the analyses don't distinguish between formation and maintenance of domains.

Both discuss the weak interaction observed in the control transgene without homie (C142-C144). OpenEval finds this SUPPORTED as an unexpected finding, and peer reviewers also rate it SUPPORTED, accepting it as baseline demonstrating boundary elements are required for functional interactions.

Both address functional implications of loop topology for gene regulation (C188-C193). OpenEval finds the distance-dependence and topological constraints SUPPORTED by live imaging studies, and peer reviewers also rate this SUPPORTED, not challenging the mechanistic context.
OpenEval finds the background on competing models (C1-C7) SUPPORTED as established knowledge. No corresponding peer review evaluation addresses these introductory claims about the two models.
OpenEval finds the TAD organization between transgene and eve locus (C87-C91) SUPPORTED by MicroC data. No specific peer review evaluation addresses these structural observations.
OpenEval finds the hierarchical LDC domain organization (C92-C95) SUPPORTED. While peer R10 touches on some LDC claims, it focuses on mechanisms rather than the basic organizational observations.

OpenEval finds the absence of volcano plumes and stripes in neighboring TADs (C96-C99) SUPPORTED. While peer R2 addresses stripe absence broadly, it doesn't specifically evaluate these neighboring TAD observations.

OpenEval finds the absence of breakthrough signatures and reduced LDC incorporation (C100-C103) SUPPORTED as evidence against loop extrusion. While peer R2 addresses stripe absence generally, it doesn't specifically evaluate the LDC incorporation claims.
OpenEval finds the competing model predictions clearly articulated (C118-C120) and SUPPORTED. No peer review evaluation specifically addresses these predictive framework claims.

OpenEval finds the negative control without homie (C121-C123) SUPPORTED. While peer R14 addresses the control with weak interaction (C142-C144), it doesn't evaluate the complete absence claims C121-C123.

OpenEval finds the GeimohL expression patterns (C124-C129) SUPPORTED. While peer R4 addresses some transgene expression data, it focuses on different claim combinations and doesn't specifically evaluate C124-C129 as a group.

OpenEval finds that homie orientation within transgene determines activation (C136-C141) SUPPORTED. While peer R4 addresses transgene expression broadly, it doesn't specifically evaluate these claims about internal vs. chromosomal orientation.

OpenEval finds preservation of intervening TAD organization (C149-C151) SUPPORTED as evidence against loop extrusion. While peer R2 addresses stripe absence, it doesn't specifically evaluate the intact TAD structure claims.

OpenEval finds virtual 4C results showing dual interactions (C152-C154) SUPPORTED. While peer R5 addresses MicroC correlations broadly, it doesn't specifically evaluate the virtual 4C dual pairing interpretation.

OpenEval finds that reversing homie switches both functional and physical patterns (C155-C159) SUPPORTED. While peer R5 addresses MicroC-expression correlations, it doesn't specifically evaluate the orientation reversal effects as a distinct claim set.

OpenEval finds the G-series transgene patterns (C160-C164) SUPPORTED, with the absence of eveGa TAD being particularly strong evidence. No peer review evaluation specifically addresses the G-series results.

OpenEval rates speculation about vertebrate generalizability (C194) as UNCERTAIN, noting lack of direct experimental evidence. No peer review evaluation addresses this speculative claim about vertebrates.
